answers.1: The main objects are commits: a known good commit (bug absent), a known bad commit (bug present), and the first bad commit (the earliest commit where the bug is present). The others are the midpoint commit that git checks out, the range of suspect commits, the bisect session (started with start, ended with reset), the marks (good, bad, skip), and, when automated, a test command whose exit code becomes the mark.
answers.2: A good commit and a bad commit mark the two ends of the suspect range. The first bad commit lies after the good end and at or before the bad end. Git checks out the midpoint. Your mark on it decides which half still holds the first bad commit: bad means at or before the midpoint, good means after it. The next midpoint is taken inside that half. Skip makes git pick a nearby commit instead. With `git bisect run`, the command's exit code supplies the mark: 0 is good, 125 is skip, and any other value from 1 to 127 is bad.
answers.3: Each good or bad mark on the midpoint rules out half of the suspects. This works because the bug is assumed to appear once and stay. Repeated halving shrinks the range to a single commit, the first bad commit.
answers.4: The most important variable is the number of commits in the range. Doubling it adds only about one more test, because each test halves the range: the test count grows like the number of halvings needed to reach 1 (about 10 for 1,000), not like the number of commits. A second variable is whether the bug stays once it appears. If it comes and goes, a good result at the midpoint can wrongly throw away the half that holds the real first appearance, and bisect names a later commit.
answers.5: Assumption: the bug appears once and stays present in every later commit. Established fact: in the document's example, bisecting 1,000 commits names 900, even though the bug first appeared at 300.
answers.6: git bisect finds the earliest commit where a bug is present by binary search between a known good commit and a known bad commit. You start a session, mark bad and good, and git checks out the midpoint. You test it and mark it good or bad, which discards half the suspects, and you repeat until git prints the first bad commit. Then `git bisect reset` returns you to your branch. Untestable commits can be skipped, and `git bisect run` can automate the test through exit codes. The result is only reliable if the bug appeared once and stayed: about 10 tests cover 1,000 commits, but an intermittent bug can lead bisect to a later commit.
answers.7: The Limit example was hardest to follow. It is unclear why 'testing next to 900 does not reveal this', and the fix (find a bad commit like 350 by spot-checking, then bisect again) arrives quickly. A small diagram of the good and bad regions on a line from 0 to 1,000 would make it easier, as would saying how many spot checks are enough. The skip section is also thin: it never says what happens if the skipped commit is itself the culprit.
answers.8: About 10. Each test halves the suspects: 1,000 → 500 → 250 → 125 → 63 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. A one-by-one search could need up to 1,000 tests.
answers.9: Run `git bisect skip`, and git selects a nearby commit to test instead. In automated mode, have the command exit with code 125 to skip. The explanation does not say what happens if the skipped commit turns out to be the first bad commit.
answers.10: When the bug does not appear once and stay, so it comes and goes across history. A midpoint can then test good even though an earlier region was bad, and bisect discards that region. In automated mode, a test that fails for some other reason also marks a commit bad, which can mislead the search.
answers.11: When the bug comes and goes. Example: across 1,000 commits the bug is present in 300–400, absent after that, and back from 900. The first test, at 500, is good, so bisect searches only 500–1,000 and names 900, but the bug first appeared at 300. To catch this, test a few commits spread across earlier history. Here 350 is bad, and bisecting between a good commit before 300 and 350 names 300. A second case: with `git bisect run`, a command that fails for an unrelated reason marks a commit bad.
